title: What is a Unix timestamp? Epoch time explained with examples — cv.cm
description: A Unix timestamp counts seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. See how it is calculated, seconds vs milliseconds, leap seconds and the 2038 problem.
answer: A Unix timestamp is the number of seconds that have passed since 00:00:00 UTC on 1 January 1970, called the Unix epoch, not counting leap seconds. It is a single integer with no time zone attached, so `1700000000` means the same instant everywhere: 14 November 2023, 22:13:20 UTC. JavaScript and many APIs use milliseconds instead, which makes the number three digits longer.

body: POSIX defines "seconds since the epoch" with a fixed formula: every day counts as exactly 86,400 seconds, and the count starts at `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z`. Moments before the epoch are negative, so `-1` is `1969-12-31T23:59:59Z`.

Because the value is measured in UTC, it carries no time zone and no daylight saving time. Converting it to a wall-clock time is a separate step that needs a zone, for example `Asia/Tokyo` or `America/New_York`.
The classic Unix timestamp is in seconds, but many systems store finer units. The digit count is the quickest way to tell them apart for current dates:

body: Mixing units is the most common timestamp bug. A seconds value passed to JavaScript's `new Date()` lands in January 1970; a milliseconds value read as seconds lands tens of thousands of years in the future. In JavaScript, convert with `Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000)` to get seconds, and `new Date(seconds * 1000)` to go back.

UTC occasionally inserts a leap second to stay in step with the Earth's rotation; 27 have been added since 1972. Unix time ignores them: the POSIX formula assumes every day has 86,400 seconds, so a leap second is either repeated or smeared across a longer period, depending on the system.

In practice this means subtracting two timestamps gives elapsed time that can be off by the number of leap seconds in between. For everyday scheduling that error does not matter; for scientific or financial timing, systems use TAI or GPS time instead. International timekeeping bodies voted in 2022 to stop adding leap seconds by 2035.

Older software stores Unix time in a signed 32-bit integer, whose maximum is `2147483647`. That value is reached at `2038-01-19T03:14:07Z`. One second later the counter overflows to `-2147483648`, which reads as `1901-12-13T20:45:52Z`.

ul: Modern 64-bit operating systems, languages and databases use a 64-bit `time_t`, which lasts for about 292 billion years.
Risk remains in embedded devices, old file formats, 32-bit database columns such as MySQL `TIMESTAMP`, and binary protocols that reserve only four bytes for a time.
Long-dated values such as 20-year certificates, mortgages and expiry dates already cross 2038, so the bug can appear well before that date.

body.note: JavaScript is not affected in the same way: a `Date` holds milliseconds in a 64-bit float and is valid up to the year 275760.

sections.h: When to use a timestamp and when to use a date string
body: Store instants (when an event happened, when a token expires) as a Unix timestamp or as a UTC date string. Both are unambiguous and sort correctly.

Use a human-readable ISO 8601 string such as `2026-10-14T09:30:00Z` in logs, APIs and files that people will read, because `1791970200` means nothing at a glance. Keep future local events, like a meeting at 09:00 in Paris next spring, as a local time plus an IANA zone name: daylight saving rules can change before the date arrives, and a precomputed timestamp would then be wrong.

faq.q: Is a Unix timestamp always in UTC?
faq.a: Yes. The count is defined from midnight UTC on 1 January 1970, so the number itself has no time zone. Only the conversion to a readable local time depends on a zone.

faq.q: How do I get the current Unix timestamp?
faq.a: Run `date +%s` in a Linux or macOS terminal, `Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000)` in JavaScript, or `int(time.time())` in Python. All return seconds since the epoch.

faq.q: Why does my timestamp convert to a date in 1970?
faq.a: The value is almost certainly in seconds but was read as milliseconds. Multiply it by 1,000 before passing it to a function that expects milliseconds, such as JavaScript's `new Date()`.

faq.q: Can a Unix timestamp be negative?
faq.a: Yes. Negative values count backwards from the epoch, so `-86400` is 31 December 1969 at 00:00 UTC. Some older systems reject them, so test before storing pre-1970 dates this way.
